title: Learn a language, or the owl finds you
description: Duolingo extended its unhinged-mascot bit — including a staged 'death' of Duo the owl and a cameo-style tie-in around Dua Lipa's album cycle — leaning entirely on organic-feeling stunts rather than traditional media spend. The strategy mirrors the brand's long-running approach of treating its app-store notifications and social account as the actual ad unit.

images.caption: Duolingo — Learn a language, or the owl finds you

title: It's CeraVe. He's Michael Cera. Coincidence?
description: CeraVe built a mockumentary-style campaign around the coincidence of Michael Cera's name, running teaser content for weeks before revealing the joke in a Super Bowl spot. It's a rare case of a clinical, dermatologist-endorsed skincare brand using absurdist celebrity comedy instead of the category's usual efficacy-first messaging.

images.caption: CeraVe — It's CeraVe. He's Michael Cera. Coincidence?

title: Like a good neighbor, Jake is there
description: State Farm continued to lean on its 'Jake from State Farm' character, pairing him with athlete cameos across digital cutdowns rather than a single hero spot. The insurer's decade-plus consistency with the same mascot is unusual in a category that typically rotates spokespeople every few years.

images.caption: State Farm — Like a good neighbor, Jake is there

title: Convicted of loving Liquid Death too much
description: Liquid Death cast real people who had been fired, arrested, or otherwise gotten in trouble for their devotion to the brand, framing canned water with the visual language of a heavy-metal energy drink. The joke only works because the product itself is unglamorous — comedy is doing the differentiation that flavor or price would do for a normal beverage brand.

images.caption: Liquid Death — Convicted of loving Liquid Death too much

title: The soda that loves your gut back
description: Poppi paired a Super Bowl broadcast spot with a QR-code vending stunt at the stadium, betting that a functional-beverage pitch (prebiotics, low sugar) could work inside a category historically sold on nostalgia and taste. The stunt drew as much commentary for its execution and subsequent backlash as for the ad itself, a reminder that experiential add-ons carry their own reputational risk.

images.caption: Poppi — The soda that loves your gut back

title: Premium wireless. Shockingly cheap.
description: Mint Mobile kept running low-budget-styled Ryan Reynolds cutdowns direct-to-camera, a format built to look inexpensive on purpose — the joke is part of the pitch that the carrier passes savings to customers. The ongoing cadence of short, meme-ready clips is built for the Ad Library format as much as for TV.

images.caption: Mint Mobile — Premium wireless. Shockingly cheap.

title: The dawn of a new AI
description: OpenAI's first paid Super Bowl spot leaned on sweeping, humanist imagery rather than a product demo, treating ChatGPT as a moment-of-history event instead of a software feature. It's a notable pivot for a company that grew almost entirely on word-of-mouth and developer buzz, now buying attention alongside legacy consumer brands.

images.caption: OpenAI — The dawn of a new AI

title: Skip the search. Get the answer.
description: Perplexity's paid social creative positions the product directly against traditional search — screenshots of a cluttered results page next to a clean cited answer — rather than explaining what an 'AI answer engine' is from scratch. The direct-comparison format is a common challenger-brand move: define yourself by what you replace, not what you are.

images.caption: Perplexity — Skip the search. Get the answer.

title: The card that pays you back
description: Robinhood's Gold Card launch ads used a waitlist-and-scarcity framing — a physical card with a visible serial number — to borrow the cachet of exclusive credit products while undercutting them on cash-back terms. The creative deliberately looks like a luxury-card ad, a departure from Robinhood's earlier, more utilitarian trading-app messaging.

images.caption: Robinhood — The card that pays you back

title: Money moves different here
description: Cash App's creative continues to run through artist and creator partnerships rather than product-feature explainers, treating the Cash Card's design drops as a cultural object first and a debit card second. The approach mirrors streetwear marketing more than fintech marketing, which is part of how the brand differentiates from Venmo and Zelle.

images.caption: Cash App — Money moves different here

title: Unlock your body's data
description: Whoop's ads foreground recovery and strain scores over step counts, targeting a more data-literate fitness audience than the broader wearables market. The subscription-hardware model (the band itself is nominally free with membership) is unusual enough that a chunk of the creative has to do the work of explaining the business model, not just the device.

title: The tumbler that survived a burning car
description: Stanley's marketing largely amplified a customer's own viral video of a Quencher tumbler surviving a car fire with the ice inside still intact, rather than originating the moment itself — the brand's paid media picked up and re-cut existing organic content. It's a case study in a 100-year-old outdoor-gear company repositioning around limited-edition colorways and collector culture instead of durability alone.

images.caption: Stanley — The tumbler that survived a burning car

title: This week's flavors are already gone
description: Crumbl's ads are structured entirely around scarcity and a weekly release cadence, mirroring sneaker-drop marketing more than fast-casual food marketing. The rotating menu gives the brand a reason to post new creative every single week without needing a new campaign concept — the calendar is the campaign.

images.caption: Crumbl — This week's flavors are already gone

title: One scoop, foundational nutrition
description: AG1 (formerly Athletic Greens) rebranded around the vaguer, more defensible term 'foundational nutrition' rather than specific health claims, a common move for supplement brands navigating regulatory scrutiny. Its ad creative leans heavily on subscription-and-ritual framing — the daily scoop as habit — over any single ingredient story.

title: Add it to the cart
description: Instacart's Super Bowl spot built its visual gag around edible art made from grocery items, a way to make a fundamentally logistics-driven service (delivery, routing, warehouses) feel colorful and food-forward on screen. The category's ads increasingly compete on the emotional register of home cooking rather than convenience or speed alone.

images.caption: Instacart — Add it to the cart
